title: Breaking Two Hours: The Story of the Marathon World Record and What Comes Next
summary: Eliud Kipchoge's sub-two-hour marathon — first achieved unofficially in 2019, then ratified as a world record in 2023 — is one of sport's greatest achievements. We look at the history of the world record and how far human endurance can go.
content:
For decades, the two-hour marathon was sport's equivalent of the four-minute mile: a barrier that experts declared physiologically impossible, that runners spent careers approaching but never crossing, that existed in the sport's imagination as the ultimate test of what human endurance could achieve.

Eliud Kipchoge crossed it. And in doing so, he did not simply set a record — he redefined what was possible, in athletics and perhaps in human endeavour more broadly.

The History of the Record

The marathon world record has fallen steadily over the past century, driven by better training methods, improved nutrition science, superior footwear technology, and — crucially — an expanding global talent pool that has brought East African runners to the forefront of the event.

When Abebe Bikila ran barefoot to Olympic gold in Rome in 1960, his time of 2:15:16 was the world record. The idea that a human being might run 26.2 miles in under two hours would have seemed not just unlikely but physically absurd. The physiological demands — the energy expenditure, the cardiovascular strain, the muscular wear across two hours of sustained maximum effort — were considered to place a hard ceiling on what was achievable.

Kipchoge and the Sub-Two

Eliud Kipchoge's 2019 Ineos 1:59 Challenge — a controlled attempt on a specially designed course in Vienna, with pacemakers and optimal conditions — produced a time of 1:59:40. Technically, it did not count as a world record under World Athletics rules because of the assistance provided. But it proved the physiological question: a human being could run a marathon in under two hours.

Four years later, at the Berlin Marathon — a course famous for its flatness and its fast conditions — Kipchoge ran 2:00:35 in a standard race setting. It was not sub-two. But it was the official world record, and it came within touching distance of the barrier that had seemed impossible.

No human is limited. That is what I wanted to show the world. The barrier is not in our legs or our lungs. It is in our minds. When you remove the mental barrier, the physical barrier goes with it.

The Shoe Revolution

The improvement in marathon times over the past decade cannot be separated from the revolution in footwear technology. Carbon-fibre plated running shoes — pioneered by Nike and now produced by every major manufacturer — improve running economy by several percentage points. The legal debate about where technology ends and unfair advantage begins continues, but the practical reality is that modern marathon shoes have made fast times more accessible to more runners than any previous innovation.

Who Comes After Kipchoge?

Kipchoge is 41. The next generation of East African distance runners — Kenyans and Ethiopians who have grown up watching him redefine the possible — are already pushing at the limits of what his records established. Kelvin Kiptum's 2023 Berlin time of 2:00:35 that was ratified as the world record came from a 23-year-old in just his third marathon.

The sub-two barrier in a standard race — without the controlled conditions of Vienna — may be closer than anyone imagined. And when it falls, it will be one of sport's defining moments.
